issue.title: write_file fails for Sub-Agents
issue.body:
There is a very nasty bug in v0.8.46+ where write_file fails for Sub-Agents about 90% of the time. Sub-Agents that are told to use the write_file tool will end up writing nothing, even though they may think that the write succeded. This is a big problem for "map-reduce" workflows where the main Orchestrator Agent spins up many Sub-Agents and askes them to do work and write their results to disk before collecting everything. These workflows don't work at all in Codewhale. It took a while but I've managed to fix the problem in my fork. We certainly want to fix them on main. The attached HTML files and the patch describe the problem in detail and the solution. [writefile-is-flaky.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28477209/writefile-is-flaky.patch) Github is so unbelievably awful. It doesn't allow me to attach .xhtml files so I will paste them here. Copy and paste these files into your own workspace to begin your analysis. :problem.xhtml Problem: write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Problem: write_file is broken in CodeWhale Sub-Agents

Summary

The write_file tool is available in sub-agent sessions but is deeply unreliable. Out of approximately 60 combined invocations across three sub-agents during testing, it produced one file with 6 lines of content, two files with three dots (...), and zero-content failures for all remaining calls. Sub-agents self-report that write_file renders with empty parameters. This makes it impossible for sub-agents to reliably write research reports or any file exceeding a few bytes to disk.

Observed Behavior — Detailed Test Results

Three research sub-agents were launched in parallel to research INTC stock. They were instructed to write findings to a markdown file using write_file.

Test results
Sub-AgentOutput FileStepsDurationStatusFile ContentsFailed Attempts
intc-price-action intc-price-action.md 73 19 min Completed 6 lines — title + partial content ~35 (self-reported)
intc-analyst-sentiment intc-analyst-sentiment.md 40 15 min Completed 1 line: ... ~25 (self-reported)
intc-news-catalysts intc-news-catalysts.md 0 22 min Failed (SSE timeout) 1 line: ... Unknown

intc-price-action

Self-reported write_file always rendering with empty parameters across ~35 attempts. One attempt produced 6 lines. The full research was delivered in the agent_eval summary instead.

intc-analyst-sentiment

First invocation succeeded in writing ..., and 25+ subsequent invocations failed silently. The agent stated: Unfortunately, the write_file tool has been malfunctioning across 25+ attempts — only one early invocation succeeded (writing "..." to the file).

intc-news-catalysts

Queued behind others and starved of concurrency, failing after 22 minutes (SSE stream timeout). Wrote exactly ... in its only attempt.

Observed Failure Modes

  1. Empty-parameter invocation: The tool call is constructed correctly by the model, but the content parameter is dropped, nullified, or truncated before the tool executes.
  2. Silent success with no content: The tool returns success: true but writes an empty file, ..., or nothing.
  3. First-write partial success, subsequent total failure: The first call might produce a few bytes, but subsequent calls produce nothing, suggesting state corruption.
  4. Intermittent partial writes: Content occasionally gets through but is severely truncated (e.g., max 6 lines observed).

Root Cause Hypothesis

The empty parameters self-report combined with the first-write-partial-success pattern strongly suggests a parameter serialization bug in the sub-agent tool-call pipeline. The content string is constructed by the sub-agent, serialized, and deserialized by the tool executor. During this pipeline, the content is lost or corrupted.

The orchestrator does not exhibit this behavior; write_file works correctly when called from the main context. The bug is strictly isolated to sub-agent sessions.

:investigation.xhtml Investigation: write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Investigation: write_file is broken in CodeWhale Sub-Agents

Root Cause Identified

The root cause is a logic error in the way streaming tool arguments are parsed, specifically an interaction between crates/tui/src/core/engine/dispatch.rs and the arg_repair module.

When the subagent streams tool arguments, they are accumulated in a buffer and parsed via parse_tool_input. In dispatch.rs, this function first attempts to use crate::tools::arg_repair::repair(trimmed) to fix any malformed JSON. If this fails, it is supposed to fall back to legacy strategies like strip_code_fences and extract_json_segment.

However, arg_repair::repair is implemented such that if all 5 of its repair stages fail, it falls back to returning an empty JSON object (Ok(Value::Object(Map::new()))) rather than an error. Because it returns Ok, parse_tool_input assumes the repair was successful and returns the empty object, bypassing the legacy fallbacks entirely.

How This Causes the Observed Behavior

  1. Subagents, being LLMs, frequently output their tool arguments wrapped in markdown code fences (e.g., ```json\n{ "path": "...", "content": "..." }\n```).
  2. When this fenced string is passed to arg_repair::repair, the repair ladder fails to parse it since it contains markdown.
  3. Instead of returning an error, repair silently swallows the failure and returns an empty object {}.
  4. parse_tool_input receives Ok({}), skips strip_code_fences, and assigns {} as the tool's input.
  5. The tool executor receives empty parameters, fails validation, and the subagent observes that write_file received no arguments.

This explains why the subagent self-reports that write_file renders with empty parameters. The main orchestrator likely avoids this either due to stricter system prompt adherence, or because subagents generate much larger JSON payloads for write_file that trigger this fenced output format more frequently.

Proposed Fix

The repair function in crates/tui/src/tools/arg_repair.rs should be modified so that its final fallback returns a proper Err instead of Ok(Value::Object(Map::new())). This will allow parse_tool_input in dispatch.rs to correctly fall through to strip_code_fences and extract_json_segment when the arg_repair ladder fails.

Alternatively, the order of operations in parse_tool_input could be adjusted to attempt strip_code_fences before applying arg_repair.

:investigation_alternate.xhtml Alternate Investigation: write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Alternate Investigation: write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Investigation Methodology

This investigation traced the entire subagent tool-call pipeline end-to-end, from API request construction through response parsing and tool execution. The focus was on identifying architectural differences between the orchestrator (streaming) path and the subagent (non-streaming) path that could explain the systematic failure of write_file in subagents.

Key Finding: Subagents Use Non-Streaming API with a 4096-Token Hard Cap

The original investigation focused on the arg_repair module and streaming delta parsing. However, subagents do not use the streaming path at all. This is the critical architectural difference that was overlooked.

Evidence: Non-Streaming Request

In crates/tui/src/tools/subagent/mod.rs, line 3822, the subagent constructs its MessageRequest with:

stream: Some(false),

This means the subagent receives a complete, pre-parsed JSON response from the DeepSeek API — not a stream of deltas. The response is parsed by parse_chat_message in crates/tui/src/client/chat.rs, which extracts tool_calls[].function.arguments as a string and parses it via serde_json::from_str. The arg_repair module and parse_tool_input function are never invoked for subagent tool calls.

Evidence: 4096-Token Hard Cap

In the same file, line 3815:

max_tokens: 4096,

Every subagent API request is capped at 4096 output tokens. This is a hard limit on the total response length, including thinking tokens, text content, and tool call arguments. When the model emits a write_file tool call, the content parameter (the file body) is serialized as a JSON string inside the arguments field. For any non-trivial file, this easily exceeds 4096 tokens.

Evidence: Silent Truncation

When the API response is truncated by the max_tokens limit, DeepSeek sets finish_reason: "length" instead of "tool_calls" or "stop". The truncated response contains a partial tool_calls array with an incomplete arguments JSON string. The critical finding is in parse_chat_message (line 1810-1813):

let arguments = function
    .and_then(|f| f.get("arguments"))
    .and_then(Value::as_str)
    .map(|raw| serde_json::from_str(raw).unwrap_or(Value::String(raw.to_string())))
    .unwrap_or(Value::Null);

When the arguments string is truncated mid-JSON (e.g., {"path": "/tmp/report.md", "content": "# Report\n\nThis is the...), serde_json::from_str fails and the code falls back to Value::String(raw.to_string()). This wraps the raw truncated string as a JSON string value. The write_file tool then calls required_str(&input, "content"), which looks for a "content" key in the input object — but the input is now a Value::String, not a Value::Object. This causes required_str to return a MissingField error.

Furthermore, the subagent loop (lines 3891-3903) does not check response.stop_reason. It never detects the "length" truncation. It blindly processes whatever partial tool calls were deserialized, leading to silent failures.

How This Causes the Observed Behavior

  1. The subagent LLM decides to call write_file with a multi-line content parameter (e.g., a research report).
  2. The serialized tool call arguments easily exceed 4096 tokens. The API truncates the response mid-JSON.
  3. parse_chat_message receives the truncated arguments string. serde_json::from_str fails. The fallback wraps the raw string as Value::String.
  4. The write_file tool receives Value::String("...") instead of Value::Object({"path": ..., "content": ...}). It fails with a missing field error.
  5. The subagent sees the error, retries, and hits the same 4096-token wall every time.
  6. The occasional "success" with ... or 6 lines of content occurs when the model produces a short enough response (e.g., a placeholder or stub) that fits within the 4096-token budget.

Why the Orchestrator Does Not Have This Problem

The main orchestrator uses the streaming path (stream: true) and does not set max_tokens: 4096. It processes tool call arguments incrementally via InputJsonDelta chunks and the input_buffer accumulation in turn_loop.rs. Even if the model emits thousands of tokens for a write_file content parameter, the streaming path accumulates them all. The arg_repair and parse_tool_input functions are invoked during streaming to progressively parse the growing buffer. This is why write_file works perfectly from the orchestrator.

Why the Original Fix Did Not Help

The original investigation and fix targeted arg_repair.rs (the empty-object fallback) and dispatch.rs (the parse_tool_input reordering and newline escaping). These changes are correct and valuable for the streaming path, but subagents never touch these code paths. Subagents use stream: Some(false) and parse_chat_message — an entirely separate pipeline. The fix was applied to the wrong pipeline.

Additional Supporting Evidence

  • Step count correlation: The "intc-price-action" subagent took 73 steps with ~35 failed write_file attempts. Each failed attempt consumed at least one step (tool call + error). This is consistent with repeated truncation — the model keeps retrying because the error message says "missing field", not "output too long".
  • Partial success pattern: The one file that got 6 lines of content suggests the model tried writing a very short version that happened to fit within 4096 tokens. The ... outputs were likely even shorter stubs.
  • Self-report of "empty parameters": This is consistent with Value::Null (the .unwrap_or(Value::Null) fallback) being passed to the tool executor when the arguments field is completely absent from a severely truncated response.

Conclusion

The root cause is not a JSON parsing bug. It is an architectural limitation: subagents are hardcoded to max_tokens: 4096 with non-streaming API calls and no truncation detection. Any write_file call with a content parameter exceeding ~3000 characters will be silently truncated by the API, producing a corrupted tool call that fails at the tool executor level.

:proposal_alternate.xhtml Alternate Proposal: Fix write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Alternate Proposal: Fix write_file Flakiness in Sub-Agents

Objective

Fix the subagent write_file flakiness by increasing the max_tokens limit for subagent API requests and adding truncation detection to the subagent step loop. The root cause is that subagents are hardcoded to max_tokens: 4096 with non-streaming API calls, which silently truncates any write_file call whose content parameter exceeds approximately 3000 characters.

Required Changes

1. Increase max_tokens in Subagent Requests

File: crates/tui/src/tools/subagent/mod.rs

Change the hardcoded max_tokens: 4096 on line 3815 to a significantly larger value. The DeepSeek V4 API supports up to 16384 output tokens. Use 16384 to give subagents maximum room for large tool call arguments.

Before:

            max_tokens: 4096,

After:

            max_tokens: 16384,

2. Detect Truncation in the Subagent Step Loop

File: crates/tui/src/tools/subagent/mod.rs

After receiving the API response and before processing tool calls, check response.stop_reason. If it equals "length", do not attempt to execute the tool calls (they are likely truncated and corrupt). Instead, inject a synthetic tool error result into the conversation so the model knows the response was truncated and can retry with a shorter output.

Insert the following check after line 3889 (after the usage reporting block), before the for block in &response.content loop:

        // Detect API-level truncation. When stop_reason is "length", the
        // response was cut short by max_tokens and any tool_calls are likely
        // corrupted (truncated JSON arguments). Skip tool execution and
        // inject a synthetic error so the model can retry with shorter output.
        let truncated = response
            .stop_reason
            .as_deref()
            .map_or(false, |r| r == "length");

Then, in the tool execution section (around line 3939), wrap the tool execution in a truncation guard:

        if truncated && !tool_uses.is_empty() {
            emit_agent_progress(
                runtime.event_tx.as_ref(),
                runtime.mailbox.as_ref(),
                &agent_id,
                format!("step {steps}/{max_steps}: response truncated by max_tokens, skipping {} tool call(s)", tool_uses.len()),
            );
            for (tool_id, tool_name, _) in &tool_uses {
                tool_results.push(ContentBlock::ToolResult {
                    tool_use_id: tool_id.clone(),
                    content: format!(
                        "Error: Your response was truncated by the max_tokens limit before the tool call arguments for '{}' could be fully generated. \
                         Reduce the size of the 'content' parameter (e.g., write a shorter file, split into multiple smaller writes, or summarize) and retry.",
                        tool_name
                    ),
                    is_error: Some(true),
                    content_blocks: None,
                });
            }
            // Skip the normal tool execution below
            tool_uses.clear();
        }

Why This Works

  1. Raising max_tokens to 16384 gives the model 4x more room for tool call arguments, which is sufficient for most research reports and file content that subagents need to write.
  2. Truncation detection catches the edge case where even 16384 tokens is insufficient. Instead of silently executing a corrupted tool call (which writes an empty or garbled file), the subagent receives a clear error message explaining the truncation. The model can then retry with shorter content or split the write across multiple calls.

Expected Outcome

Subagents will be able to reliably write files up to approximately 12000 characters (the portion of the 16384-token budget available after system prompt, thinking, and JSON overhead). For larger files, the truncation detection will give the model an actionable error message instead of a silent failure, allowing it to adapt its strategy.

Risk Assessment

  • Cost impact: Raising max_tokens does not increase cost unless the model actually generates more tokens. DeepSeek bills per output token, not per max_tokens capacity. The vast majority of subagent steps (tool calls that are not write_file) will continue to use far fewer than 4096 tokens.
  • Latency impact: Subagent responses may take slightly longer for large write_file calls since the model is now allowed to generate more tokens. This is acceptable because the alternative is a failed call that wastes the entire step.
  • Backward compatibility: Both changes are backward-compatible. Existing subagent behavior is preserved for all tool calls that fit within 4096 tokens.

steps: Use three sub-agents to prepare separate local Markdown reports about the INTC stock research workflow: price action, analyst sentiment, and news catalysts. Each sub-agent should write its own findings with write_file to intc-price-action.md, intc-analyst-sentiment.md, or intc-news-catalysts.md. Use only information available locally and clearly identify information you cannot obtain. Collect the reports afterwards.
expected: Sub-agent write_file calls retain complete arguments and produce the requested reports, or explicitly report a generation/truncation error.
defect: Sub-agent responses hit a fixed output-token ceiling; incomplete write_file arguments are dispatched as non-object input and repeatedly fail or produce short placeholders.

fault location.explanation: The issue corrects its original streaming hypothesis: sub-agents use non-streaming completions with max_tokens=4096. Truncated JSON arguments fall back to a string in parse_chat_message, while the sub-agent loop does not reject finish_reason=length before dispatch. This is an issue-derived mechanism, not a new runtime observation.

Root cause: The issue corrects its original streaming hypothesis: sub-agents use non-streaming completions with max_tokens=4096. Truncated JSON arguments fall back to a string in parse_chat_message, while the sub-agent loop does not reject finish_reason=length before dispatch. This is an issue-derived mechanism, not a new runtime observation.
